questions.question: Describe the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient for South Africa, then evaluate the main redistribution instruments with a limitation for each.
questions.expected_answer: The Lorenz curve lines the population up from poorest to richest along the bottom and plots the cumulative share of income they hold up the side; perfect equality is the straight diagonal, and reality sags below it — the deeper the sag, the worse the inequality. The Gini coefficient scores the sag between zero and one, and South Africa's, around 0,65, is among the highest ever recorded. Instruments with mechanisms and limits: progressive taxation takes higher percentages from higher incomes but needs a growing base; social grants reach millions of households as the most direct poverty relief but depend on that tax base; free basic services cover water and electricity for the poor; the minimum wage lifts the floor but only under those employed; land reform and empowerment redistribute assets but fail without finance and skills attached. The mature conclusion: redistribution needs growth to fund it and growth needs redistribution to widen it — the pot must grow while the shares move.

questions.question: Distinguish growth from development using the HDI, sketch the portrait of a developing country, and evaluate South Africa's succession of development plans.
questions.expected_answer: Growth is the increase in real GDP; development is the broader improvement in how people live — health, education, freedom and opportunity — so growth without development is possible. The HDI combines life expectancy, education and income per person, letting a healthier, better-schooled country outrank a richer one. The developing-country portrait: low income per capita, high population growth and young populations, high unemployment, dependence on primary exports, dualism — modern cities beside subsistence countryside — and thin infrastructure and human capital. South Africa fits parts of the portrait and breaks others, which honest essays state both ways. The plans run RDP for basic needs, GEAR for stability, AsgiSA for constraints, and the NDP as the current framework; the recurring evaluation is strong diagnosis, weak implementation. Indigenous knowledge systems add development from within — low-cost, locally fitted, community-owned.

questions.question: Explain how externalities and the commons cause environmental market failure, match the policy tools to the failures, and define sustainability with South Africa's stake.
questions.expected_answer: An externality lands costs on outsiders to the transaction: the smoke priced at zero makes the product too cheap, so society gets too much of it. Commons — shared rivers, grazing, fisheries — are overused because each user's gain is private while the loss is shared: what belongs to everyone is cared for by no one. Tools by failure: command and control sets enforceable standards but is blunt; market instruments restore the missing price — South Africa's carbon tax makes polluters pay, tradeable permits cap totals and locate reductions where cheapest, subsidies reward clean choices; property rights and community management give commons a guardian; agreements matter because pollution ignores borders. Sustainability is meeting present needs without compromising future generations — living off nature's interest, not its capital — on three legs: economic, social, environmental. South Africa's stake: water scarcity, faster-than-average warming, drought and flood damage, coal dependence facing border carbon taxes, and acid mine drainage.
